One Cadence brain plays Super Mario Bros. in order, 1-1, 1-2, 1-3, ..., learning the whole time and never reset between levels. The test is first sight: 3 solo attempts on a level before any practice on it. If it were learning to play Mario rather than memorizing levels, first-sight distance would rise and beat simple baselines.

Result so far: it does not. Neither brain beat the best baseline at first sight on any new level. Random buttons or an untrained brain went as far or further. No level was cleared solo. Practice helped on some levels (blind: 1-3 to 746, 2-2 to 1,496) and did nothing on others (1-2, 1-4).

Before: the blind brain saw 26 x 32 grey blocks, 2 frames, nothing else. It began from last night's 1-1 training, so its 1-1 is not a real first sight. It forgot old levels fast: 1-1 went from 898 to about 300 after practising 1-2.

After: a fresh brain with better senses. Eyes: 4 x 4 pixel blocks (4x the detail) plus how the last 3 frames changed, each frame normalized to its own background and contrast so overground, underground and castles look alike. Body sense: Mario's own speed, rising or falling, on the ground or not, facing, size, hurt and star timers, time left. From scratch it reached 594 on 1-1 in 40 minutes, then little else moved.
Boundary: the body sense comes from the game's memory, but only about Mario himself. No enemy, block or pit positions are read; the world comes from the eyes.

Practice on a level: it plays on its own and learns from the reward (going right, not dying), copies its own good stretches, and gets a few coached tries where a look-ahead planner writes down what it would have pressed. The planner never takes the controls. About a tenth of its play is an earlier level again. It moves on after a solo clear (flag in 2 of 3) or about 38 minutes.
